title: Join-slice attachment of a simplex to a full subcategory
statement:
Use small simplicial sets, full subcategories and quasicategories of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], joins of [def-coef-infinity-relative-cone], join slices of [lem-coef-infinity-slice-right-fibration], and categorical equivalences of [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]. Let $\mathcal V$ be a small quasicategory, $\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal V$ a full subcategory, and $\sigma:\Delta^r\to\mathcal V$ a nondegenerate simplex with no vertex in $\mathcal U$. Put $X=\mathcal U\times_{\mathcal V}\mathcal V_{/\sigma}$. Let $K$ be the simplicial subset generated by simplices whose vertices split into an initial block forming a simplex of $\mathcal U$ and a final block factoring through $\sigma$; either block may be empty. Let $K_\partial$ be the analogous subset requiring the final block to factor through $\partial\Delta^r$. Evaluation of a join slice defines a natural comparison
$$K_\partial\amalg_{X\star\partial\Delta^r}(X\star\Delta^r)\longrightarrow K.$$
This map is a monomorphism and a categorical equivalence. The opposite assertion holds for a simplex followed by a terminal block in a full subcategory, using $X=\mathcal V_{\sigma/}\times_{\mathcal V}\mathcal U$ and the comparison $K_\partial\amalg_{\partial\Delta^r\star X}(\Delta^r\star X)\to K$. Both assertions include $r=0$ and $X=\varnothing$; the simplex map need not embed its boundary.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.2.5, printed pp.332-333, and its opposite. This is the explicit trivial-cofibration comparison, rather than just a homotopy-pushout slogan. September 18, 2017 edition inspected online. WANTED: archive in literature/. No Stacks tag states this quasicategorical assertion.

proof.text: Write $\sigma\epsilon$ for the simplex obtained from $\sigma$ by a surjective monotone map $\epsilon:[m]\twoheadrightarrow[r]$. The unique nondegenerate decomposition of [lem-weil-pbc-simplicial-set-nondegenerate-decomposition] says that different such maps give different simplices and that none of them factors through a proper face of $\Delta^r$. Let $S$ be this set of degeneracies, ordered first by dimension, then in any order within a dimension. Each dimension contributes finitely many maps, so this is a small well-order with least member $\sigma$. Let its order type be $\alpha$. For $0\leq\beta\leq\alpha$, define $F_\beta$ to be the subcomplex generated by the nondegenerate simplices whose initial block lies in $\mathcal U$ and whose final block either factors through $\partial\Delta^r$ or is a member of $S$ earlier than $\beta$. The empty final block is included in the boundary case, so $\mathcal U\subseteq F_0$. Faces that no longer cover all vertices of $\sigma$ belong to the boundary case; a proper face still covering them has a strictly smaller tail dimension. Thus this construction is increasing and continuous at limit ordinals. The unique nondegenerate decomposition also shows $F_0=K_\partial$ and $F_\alpha=K$: if the total simplex is degenerate, first remove its degeneracies; its remaining final block still factors through $\sigma$ or its boundary.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.2.5, printed pp. 332–333; first paragraph of the proof: the set S and the filtration K_beta.

proof.text: The join-slice formula [lem-coef-infinity-slice-right-fibration] gives evaluation $X\star\Delta^r\to\mathcal V$: an $a$-simplex $x$ of $X$ is a map $\Delta^a\star\Delta^r\to\mathcal V$ with fixed final face $\sigma$ and initial face in $\mathcal U$, and evaluation restricts it along the labels in the two join factors. Its pure $X$-part maps to $\mathcal U$ and its boundary part to $K_\partial$, so it gives the required comparison. This identifies its domain with $F_1$, as follows. Outside $K_\partial$ an evaluated mixed simplex has final label a surjection $\epsilon:[b]\twoheadrightarrow[r]$. The initial/final cut is unique because the two sets of vertices, those in $\mathcal U$ and those of $\sigma$, are disjoint. The tail determines $\epsilon$ uniquely by [lem-weil-pbc-simplicial-set-nondegenerate-decomposition]. A monotone section of $\epsilon$ recovers $x$ from the evaluated simplex, so evaluation is injective on the remaining mixed simplices. For a pure final simplex, equality of the evaluated simplices gives equality of their surjections onto the nondegenerate simplex $\sigma$ by the unique-decomposition lemma, so their join labels agree. If the final label is not surjective, the simplex is in $X\star\partial\Delta^r$ and is already identified with its image in $K_\partial$ by the pushout. The pure $X$-part is also in this intersection, including $r=0$ since $X\star\varnothing=X$. A simplex with surjective final label cannot land in $K_\partial$, since a proper face cannot have nondegenerate ancestor $\sigma$. Finally a nondegenerate generator with tail $\sigma$ is precisely an $a$-simplex of $X$ evaluated on the full final face. These facts give both the identification with $F_1$ and the monomorphism, even if distinct proper faces of $\sigma$ have the same image.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.2.5, printed pp. 332–333; identification of K_1 with the displayed pushout; expanded simplexwise injection and boundary check.

proof.text: Fix a successor $F_\beta\subseteq F_{\beta+1}$ with $\beta\geq1$, corresponding to $\epsilon:[m]\twoheadrightarrow[r]$. Now $m>r$. Put $D=\mathcal U\times_{\mathcal V}\mathcal V_{/\sigma\epsilon}$ and $E=\{j\mid0\leq j<m,\ \epsilon(j)=\epsilon(j+1)\}$. The finite set $E$ is nonempty. For each nonempty $T\subseteq E$, let $q_T:[m]\twoheadrightarrow[m-|T|]$ collapse precisely the adjacent pairs in $T$, and write $\epsilon=\epsilon_Tq_T$. Precomposition with $\operatorname{id}\star q_T$ embeds $D_T:=\mathcal U\times_{\mathcal V}\mathcal V_{/\sigma\epsilon_T}$ into $D$: a section of $q_T$ recovers a preimage. These are exactly the proper-surjection factorizations in the category $J_0$ of the source proof. Their intersections satisfy $D_T\cap D_R=D_{T\cup R}$. Indeed, for a degree-$a$ simplex of $D$, take its nondegenerate decomposition in $\mathcal V$ using [lem-weil-pbc-simplicial-set-nondegenerate-decomposition]. Factoring through $\operatorname{id}_{[a]}\star q_T$ means its unique degeneracy surjection identifies the final-block adjacent pairs indexed by $T$. Factoring through both quotients means it identifies the pairs in $T\cup R$, hence factors through that joint quotient. Its recovered initial face is still in $\mathcal U$ and its final face is $\sigma\epsilon_{T\cup R}$, by restricting along a section. Thus the equality is an equality of subcomplexes, not only of vertices. Set $A=\bigcup_{\varnothing\ne T\subseteq E}D_T\subseteq D$; the singleton subsets already cover $A$.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.2.5, printed pp. 332–333; proper factorization category J_0 and the union X in the source; here A is the source proof’s X, avoiding confusion with the item’s X.

proof.text: Let $v=\sigma(0)$ and $B=\mathcal U\times_{\mathcal V}\mathcal V_{/v}$. The initial-vertex restriction lemma [lem-coef-initial-poset-slice-restriction], applied to the finite ordered sets $[m]$ and $[m-|T|]$ with least vertex $0$, makes both $D\to B$ and $D_T\to B$ trivial Kan fibrations over $\mathcal U$. The triangle commutes because $q_T(0)=0$. The lemma explicitly gives lifts against every monomorphism, so the weak factorization system of [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure] makes both maps trivial Joyal fibrations and hence categorical equivalences. Two-out-of-three gives that each inclusion $D_T\to D$ is a categorical equivalence. For $R\subseteq T\subseteq E$ with $R\ne\varnothing$, the composite $D_T\hookrightarrow D_R\to B$ is $D_T\to B$. Both maps to $B$ are categorical equivalences, so two-out-of-three makes $D_T\hookrightarrow D_R$ a categorical equivalence. No surjectivity of the source map $X\to\mathcal U$ or nonemptiness is assumed.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.2.5, printed pp. 332–333; the common restriction to C′_/C and its two trivial Kan fibrations in the last displayed triangle.

proof.text: We now prove $A\hookrightarrow D$ is a categorical equivalence by finite gluing, making explicit the source’s cofibrant homotopy-colimit argument. The induction claim is: for every $T\subseteq E$ (allowing $T=\varnothing$) and every nonempty finite $I\subseteq E$, the inclusion $\bigcup_{j\in I}D_{T\cup\{j\}}\hookrightarrow D$ is a categorical equivalence. Induct simultaneously for all $T$ on $|I|$. The one-member case is Step 4, since $T\cup\{j\}$ is nonempty. For $k\notin I$, put $Y=\bigcup_{j\in I}D_{T\cup\{j\}}$ and $Z=D_{T\cup\{k\}}$. Step 3 gives $H=Y\cap Z=\bigcup_{j\in I}D_{T\cup\{k,j\}}$, so the induction hypothesis for $T\cup\{k\}$ applies to $H$. By induction $Y\to D$ and $H\to D$ are categorical equivalences, as is $Z\to D$; two-out-of-three gives $H\to Y$ a categorical equivalence. It is a monomorphism and therefore a trivial cofibration by [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]. The pushout $Y\amalg_H Z=Y\cup Z$ is degreewise the union. Closure of the left lifting class under pushouts, [lem-coef-lifting-class-closure], shows $Z\to Y\cup Z$ is a trivial cofibration. Its composite to $D$ is the already known equivalence $Z\to D$, so two-out-of-three gives $Y\cup Z\to D$ an equivalence. Taking $T=\varnothing$ and $I=E$ completes the finite induction and proves $A\hookrightarrow D$ a categorical equivalence and monomorphism.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.2.5, printed pp. 332–333; expanded finite-poset union proof of the source’s assertion X -> C′_/sigma′ is a categorical equivalence.

proof.text: Put $P=(A\star\Delta^m)\amalg_{A\star\partial\Delta^m}(D\star\partial\Delta^m)$. The ordered-block formula makes $P$ the union of these two subcomplexes of $D\star\Delta^m$, with exactly the displayed intersection, so $j:P\hookrightarrow D\star\Delta^m$ is a monomorphism. By [lem-coef-join-preserves-categorical-equivalences], Step 5 implies both $A\star\partial\Delta^m\to D\star\partial\Delta^m$ and $A\star\Delta^m\to D\star\Delta^m$ are categorical equivalences; the lemma applies to arbitrary, possibly empty factors. The first map is also mono, hence a trivial cofibration. Its pushout $A\star\Delta^m\to P$ is a trivial cofibration by [lem-coef-lifting-class-closure] and [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]. Two-out-of-three with the second joined map proves $j$ a categorical equivalence, hence a trivial cofibration. This justifies the source’s homotopy-pushout square without assuming arbitrary pushouts preserve weak equivalences.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.2.5, printed pp. 332–333; the map j and the two vertical joined equivalences in the source’s square.

proof.text: The successor $F_\beta\hookrightarrow F_{\beta+1}$ is the pushout of $j$ along evaluation, with $D,A,m$ as in Steps 3–6. Here is the identification. Each new nondegenerate generator has tail exactly $\sigma\epsilon$ and so is the evaluation of a simplex of $D$ on the entire final $\Delta^m$. A simplex on a proper face of this last factor has smaller tail dimension or factors through $\partial\Delta^r$, so is already in $F_\beta$. A total simplex degenerate in a final direction is the degeneracy of an earlier generator exactly when its $D$-label factors through one of the proper quotients $q_T$, that is, belongs to $A$. These are precisely the second kind of old simplices, those in $A\star\Delta^m$. To check completeness, remove all total degeneracies by [lem-weil-pbc-simplicial-set-nondegenerate-decomposition]. A degeneracy removed in the initial block is accounted for by the simplicial operators of $D$; a degeneracy removed in the final block must identify equal adjacent values of $\epsilon$, so factors through a nonempty $T\subseteq E$. If neither occurs, the generator is new, its disjoint-vertex block cut and its tail label are unique, and its $D$-label is recovered by evaluating the full final face. Therefore there are no further identifications or old simplices beyond $P$. This gives the asserted pushout degreewise, compatibly with all operators. Since $j$ is a trivial cofibration, the successor is a trivial cofibration by pushout closure [lem-coef-lifting-class-closure] and [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure].

source.place: Lemma 3.1.2.5, printed pp. 332–333; the assertion K_beta -> K_(beta+1) is a pushout of j, with its overlap and degeneracy check expanded.

proof.text: The base inclusion $F_1\to F_1$ is an identity. Steps 6–7 give the successor steps, and Step 1 gives $F_\lambda=\bigcup_{\gamma<\lambda}F_\gamma$ at limits. For any Joyal fibration and a lifting problem for $F_1\to F_\alpha$, construct compatible lifts recursively: retain the prescribed lift at $1$, use the successor trivial-cofibration lifting property at every successor, and at a limit define the lift on each simplex by its value at an earlier stage. These values agree because all lifts extend their predecessors. This proves the left lifting property against every Joyal fibration. The weak factorization system of [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure] therefore makes $F_1\hookrightarrow F_\alpha$ a trivial cofibration. Step 2 identified it with the item’s comparison, so both asserted properties follow.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.2.5, printed pp. 332–333; transfinite induction, including the compatible-union argument at limits.

proof.text: For the terminal-block version apply the result just proved in $\mathcal V^{\mathrm{op}}$ with $\mathcal U^{\mathrm{op}}$. Opposites of quasicategories are quasicategories by [lem-coef-infinity-relative-cone-equivalence](4). Reversing an ordered block gives $(A\star B)^{\mathrm{op}}\cong B^{\mathrm{op}}\star A^{\mathrm{op}}$, and the slice formula identifies the opposite incoming slice with the outgoing slice in the statement, including its entire remaining-face projection. Opposite reindexes degrees and hence preserves the pushout and monomorphisms. It preserves categorical equivalences directly from [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]: $\operatorname{Fun}(A^{\mathrm{op}},C)\cong\operatorname{Fun}(A,C^{\mathrm{op}})^{\mathrm{op}}$, naturally under restriction, and passing to the presented homotopy categories commutes with opposite. Thus the test for the reversed map is the opposite of the test against $C^{\mathrm{op}}$ for the original map, an equivalence of ordinary categories. No step excluded $r=0$: then $K_\partial=\mathcal U$, $\partial\Delta^0=\varnothing$, and $X\star\varnothing=X$. No step required $X$ nonempty. In particular if $X=\varnothing$, the pure factor $\Delta^r$ remains in $X\star\Delta^r$; it is not discarded. Step 4 also shows all the degeneracy slices $D$ are empty in this case, since they and $X$ map by trivial Kan fibrations onto the same $B$, and lifting $\varnothing\subseteq\Delta^0$ makes these maps surjective on vertices. The filtration adds no new mixed generators. Possible coincidences among boundary faces of $\sigma$ were absorbed in Step 2’s pushout and never assumed absent.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.2.5, printed pp. 332–333; opposite assertion and audit of the empty slice, vertex simplex, and nonembedded boundary cases.
